AGENTS.md phase-3 disclosure tells agents to file/read via the backlog CLI, but there is no discoverable backlog binary. Fix: add a bin shim / global link (or a repo wrapper), or update the disclosure to the real invocation.

content:
MCP tool names leak the client-d extraction segment (backlog_client_d_create_item, not backlog_create_item)

serve --transport mcp lists tools as backlog_client_d_<fn> (e.g. backlog_client_d_create_item). The client-d segment is the client.d.ts file-name extraction artifact cli.ts strips for the CLI transport; cli.ts DOCUMENTS that MCP routes by bare fnName and the segment is invisible there, but the live MCP tool names DO carry it. Result: the phase-3 disclosure names mcp__backlog__create_item, but the real tool is mcp__backlog__backlog_client_d_create_item, so agents cannot call the documented name. Fix: derive MCP tool names from bare fnName (drop namespace+client-d prefix) in apigen-plugin-mcp, matching what cli.ts claims.

content:
backlog tests never drive the shipped CLI/MCP commands

102 tests exercise store/client in-process; nothing runs the built bin as a consumer or the MCP tools over JSON-RPC against the packed tarball. That is why 0.0.1 shipped no bin and 0.0.2 crashed on pino-pretty in a TTY. Add pack->install->run-bin (incl pty pretty path) + MCP tools/list+call, gate in publish.

content:
apigen-cli serve/run not killable: Server.close() hangs on lingering connections, orphaning host children

serve.ts createFrontServer() wraps Node net.Server/http2.Server/http.Server close() calls, but none force-close open sockets/sessions. Node Server.close() only fires its callback once every existing connection ends on its own -- a single lingering keep-alive HTTP client or persistent gRPC/h2c session (exactly what this front proxies) hangs close() forever. shutdown() in startServe() awaited front.close() BEFORE killAll(hosts), so a hung close() meant host children (spawned via orchestrator.ts spawnHost() as `apigen run` child processes) were never sent SIGTERM either -- if the user eventually gave up and closed the terminal/SIGKILLed the top-level serve process, those children were orphaned forever (reproduced live: an orphaned `run --type api-fastify ... --namespace a` process from an earlier serve.spec.ts SIGTERM test run survived 8+ hours as PPID=1). Additionally: no SIGHUP handler was registered in either serve.ts or run.ts, so closing a terminal (which sends SIGHUP to the foreground process group) hit Node's default disposition (immediate termination) and skipped the graceful shutdown path entirely, and run.ts had no bounded deadline so a plugin whose own server.close() equivalent hangs (e.g. Fastify does not force-close keep-alive sockets by default) could hang that run process forever too.

Fix: (1) createFrontServer now tracks every accepted raw socket + h2 session and force-destroys them in the close() override before delegating to the underlying close, and the no-gRPC plain-http path uses Node's built-in closeAllConnections(); (2) shutdown() now closes the front and kills hosts CONCURRENTLY (Promise.all) under a 5s Promise.race deadline, with a last-resort SIGKILL sweep of any host still alive after the deadline; (3) registerServeCommand now also handles SIGHUP (routed through the same graceful path) and has an 8s top-level force-exit failsafe; (4) run.ts now also handles SIGHUP and bounds its own shutdown phase with a 5s force-exit deadline after any signal, independent of how the invoked plugin's own server behaves.

Verified live: built CLI (nx build apigen-cli), reproduced the close()-hang directly via a script that opens a raw socket to createFrontServer's mixed h2c/http1 listener and calls close() (hung 5s+ before the fix); reproduced the orphan via a live 8-hour-old orphaned run process discovered during investigation, confirmed it responded normally to a direct SIGTERM once isolated. After the fix: serve with an active fixture + open request exits within ~1s of SIGINT/SIGTERM with zero orphaned children (verified via ps before/after).

content:
monitoring plugin (withMetrics) should error when a task consumes too much CPU

The withMetrics instrumentation (records to metrics.json) tracks wall/subprocess time but does not guard CPU. Add a CPU-usage threshold so a task that consumes too much CPU (e.g. oversubscribed test runs) fails/warns loudly instead of silently pinning the machine. Should surface the offending task + measured CPU.

startBacklogServer HTTP mount crashes under vitest: testSilentLogger() lacks fastify-required logger methods (FST_ERR_LOG_INVALID_LOGGER)

entrypoint/backlog/src/server.ts: testSilentLogger() returns { info: noop, error: noop } cast as unknown as Logger, passed as logger into apiFastifyPlugin.run() (via startBacklogServer, options around the fastify() call at server.ts around line 294). @fastify/error validateLogger requires the logger object to also implement debug, fatal, warn, trace, child - fastify throws FST_ERR_LOG_INVALID_LOGGER (Invalid logger object provided) at startup whenever VITEST=true. Reproduced via `CI=true npx nx test backlog`: 2 tests in src/server.spec.ts ("a real HTTP GET against getItem returns real JSON matching what createItem wrote" and "POST createItem over real HTTP actually persists - a follow-up getItem sees it") fail with "server never became ready on port <n>: TypeError: fetch failed", plus an unhandled FastifyError logged in the background with code FST_ERR_LOG_INVALID_LOGGER. Fix direction: testSilentLogger must implement the full pino-shaped surface fastify validates (debug/fatal/warn/trace/child in addition to info/error). Discovered while verifying an unrelated apigen-namespace-configurable change (dropFileSegment); testSilentLogger and its startBacklogServer call site are NOT part of that change - confirmed via git diff this addition was already present/in-flight from other concurrent work on this file.

content:
verify-dist-load kept subprocess-isolated by design - do not convert to in-process

BUILD-TOOLING-METRICS-001 asked to convert verify-dist-load.mjs and check-publish-hygiene.mjs to in-process execution (mirroring deps/executors/sync|check impl.js), eliminating the outer node <script> subprocess per project. check-publish-hygiene.mjs was converted (safe: it only wraps npm pack --dry-run, a well-behaved external CLI, same pattern as eslint-check.mjs). verify-dist-load.mjs was deliberately NOT converted: unlike eslint-check.mjs/check-publish-hygiene.mjs (which shell out to trusted tools), verify-dist-load.mjs require()/import()s the ACTUAL BUILT dist/ artifact of every project in the monorepo into the calling process - arbitrary first-party code, not a trusted CLI. Running that in-process inside a shared Nx worker (which processes many project tasks across one run-many invocation) risks: (1) global/module-registry state leaking between unrelated projects verified in the same worker process, (2) a thrown async exception or a synchronous process.exit() at import time in one project's dist crashing/killing the WHOLE worker and every other queued task on it, (3) memory growth from accumulating many full dist bundles in one long-lived process. A subprocess crash today is isolated to that one task. Recommendation: keep verify-dist-load.mjs subprocess-spawned (current impl.js, unchanged) unless/until a sandboxed-worker or vm-context isolation mechanism is added specifically for this target.

Citations: [main, backlog-tooling-cluster-fix, claude, publish/release build-tooling cluster, 1: tools/nx-plugins/build/executors/verify/verify-dist-load.mjs, 2: tools/nx-plugins/build/executors/verify/impl.js, 3: tools/nx-plugins/deps/executors/sync/impl.js, 4: tools/nx-plugins/build/executors/hygiene/impl.js]

tools/nx-plugins/build/executors/publish/release-publish.mjs (moved here from the former scripts/release-publish.mjs; PUBLISHING.md references corrected 2026-07-24) has no *.spec.mjs anywhere in the repo, but its own header comment claims 'this script's own negative-control test, see scripts/test/release-publish-gate.spec.mjs' - that file does not exist (confirmed: find . -iname 'release-publish-gate*' returns nothing). The header has been corrected in place to note the gap and point here instead of asserting a false guarantee. Separately, this script wraps the RETIRED nx-release-publish / nx release publish target model (BUG-RELEASE-PUBLISH-GATE-BYPASS-001) and is not invoked by package.json's release script (which now calls nx run-many -t publish directly, the current @adhd/nx-build:publish custom-executor pipeline). It remains referenced only from PUBLISHING.md's retired-workflow doc section. Recommend either: (a) writing the real negative-control test the header claims exists (prove --projects= routes through run-many, prove unfiltered routes through nx release publish, prove a failing dependency task yields nonzero exit and no publish), or (b) removing the file + its doc references entirely now that the current pipeline doesn't call it. Do not silently leave the header's false claim in place if this file is touched again.

version task's per-package nx release changelog spawn (159 spawns/232s measured) is NOT safely batchable inside the current per-project executor

BUILD-TOOLING-METRICS-001 asked to assess batching writeChangelogEntry (tools/nx-plugins/build/executors/version/impl.js, ~line 146) so a run-many -t version invocation emits ONE `nx release changelog --projects a,b,c` call instead of one `nx release changelog <version> --projects <name>` spawn per bumped package. Assessed and NOT implemented - two real blockers, not just difficulty:

1) VERSION HETEROGENEITY: `nx release changelog <version> --projects a,b,c` takes a SINGLE version positional argument applied to every listed project. This repo's release relationship is `independent` (nx.json releaseGroups/projectsRelationship) - each package bumps to its OWN version from its OWN current version. A single batched call across differently-versioned packages is simply the wrong nx invocation shape; it would either force every package in the batch to the same version string (wrong) or require grouping calls by resulting-version-equality (rare in practice - most bumps land at different actual version numbers), which converges back toward one call per distinct version, not one call for the whole run.

2) NO CROSS-TASK ACCUMULATION POINT: each project's `version` task is a separate nx task, potentially scheduled on a different worker process, with no shared in-memory accumulator. Doing this correctly (accumulate bumped {project, fromVersion, toVersion} across the whole run-many, then emit however-many batched changelog calls, THEN gate publish on that step succeeding) requires either (a) a shared-file handoff (write to a temp manifest per task, a NEW separate step after `nx run-many -t version` reads it and emits the batched calls) restructuring the `pnpm release` script and moving the changelog-failure gate out of the per-project `version` task's own success/failure, or (b) an Nx custom orchestrator/lifecycle hook this repo does not currently have. Both are real architectural changes, not a local edit to impl.js - out of scope for a build-tooling perf pass per the instruction to not hack fragile cross-task state.

If revisited: the (a) shared-file-handoff design is the more promising direction - `version` keeps writing its own package.json bump immediately (unchanged, needed for `^version` topological ordering of DEPENDENT ranges to work at all) but stops calling `nx release changelog` itself; a new post-run-many step (part of `pnpm release`, after `nx run-many -t version` and before `nx run-many -t publish`) reads every bump recorded that run and emits one `nx release changelog` call per distinct resulting version group. This changes the release script shape and the failure-gating contract, so it needs explicit design + a human sign-off, not a drive-by fix.

Citations: [main, backlog-tooling-cluster-fix, claude, publish/release build-tooling cluster, 1: tools/nx-plugins/build/executors/version/impl.js:146-175, 2: nx.json]

BUILD-TOOLING-METRICS-001 asked to assess batching writeChangelogEntry (tools/nx-plugins/build/executors/version/impl.js, ~line 146) so a run-many -t version invocation emits ONE `nx release changelog --projects a,b,c` call instead of one `nx release changelog <version> --projects <name>` spawn per bumped package. Assessed and NOT implemented - two real blockers, not just difficulty:

1) VERSION HETEROGENEITY: `nx release changelog <version> --projects a,b,c` takes a SINGLE version positional argument applied to every listed project. This repo's release relationship is `independent` (nx.json releaseGroups/projectsRelationship) - each package bumps to its OWN version from its OWN current version. A single batched call across differently-versioned packages is simply the wrong nx invocation shape; it would either force every package in the batch to the same version string (wrong) or require grouping calls by resulting-version-equality (rare in practice - most bumps land at different actual version numbers), which converges back toward one call per distinct version, not one call for the whole run.

2) NO CROSS-TASK ACCUMULATION POINT: each project's `version` task is a separate nx task, potentially scheduled on a different worker process, with no shared in-memory accumulator. Doing this correctly (accumulate bumped {project, fromVersion, toVersion} across the whole run-many, then emit however-many batched changelog calls, THEN gate publish on that step succeeding) requires either (a) a shared-file handoff (write to a temp manifest per task, a NEW separate step after `nx run-many -t version` reads it and emits the batched calls) restructuring the `pnpm release` script and moving the changelog-failure gate out of the per-project `version` task's own success/failure, or (b) an Nx custom orchestrator/lifecycle hook this repo does not currently have. Both are real architectural changes, not a local edit to impl.js - out of scope for a build-tooling perf pass per the instruction to not hack fragile cross-task state.

If revisited: the (a) shared-file-handoff design is the more promising direction - `version` keeps writing its own package.json bump immediately (unchanged, needed for `^version` topological ordering of DEPENDENT ranges to work at all) but stops calling `nx release changelog` itself; a new post-run-many step (part of `pnpm release`, after `nx run-many -t version` and before `nx run-many -t publish`) reads every bump recorded that run and emits one `nx release changelog` call per distinct resulting version group. This changes the release script shape and the failure-gating contract, so it needs explicit design + a human sign-off, not a drive-by fix.

Citations: [main, backlog-tooling-cluster-fix, claude, publish/release build-tooling cluster, 1: tools/nx-plugins/build/executors/version/impl.js:146-175, 2: nx.json]

render-projections verify aborts when items are archived (render excludes archived, list-items includes them)

render-projections.mjs verify compares render-to-markdown (excludes metadata.archivedAt items) against list-items (includes archived) -> any archived item makes the row DIVERGED and aborts the whole render. After archive-resolved sets archivedAt on resolved items, projections can never re-render. Fix: the verify list-items side must filter archived (or use status:open) to match render-to-markdown. Until fixed, BACKLOG.md projections cannot be regenerated once items are archived.

agent-mcp's anthropic/oauth provider has no credential path wired in .mcp.json

The `anthropic` provider type in agent-mcp (used for raw-API / Claude-OAuth-token auth, distinct from the `claudecli` subprocess provider) resolves its credential via `env.resolveEnvName("ADHD_AGENT_ANTHROPIC_SECRET")`, which requires that name to be a literal env var in the agent-mcp server process's own environment - the @adhd/environment file-based cascade explicitly excludes provider-credential vars (see comment in config.ts). But .mcp.json's agent-mcp server entry only forwards ADHD_ENV_SCOPE, ADHD_AGENT_CONFIG, and ADHD_AGENT_REGISTRY_DB_PATH in its env block - there is no ADHD_AGENT_ANTHROPIC_SECRET entry, and nothing that derives it from an existing Claude OAuth token (observed locally as CLAUDE_AUTH_TOKEN in the user's shell). Result: a real mcp__agent-mcp__task call against an anthropic-provider agent fails immediately with 'No credential for anthropic; set ADHD_AGENT_ANTHROPIC_SECRET', even when the user has a working OAuth token available under a different variable name - the live-oauth e2e test path (entrypoint/agent-mcp/src/__tests__/integration/live-oauth.e2e.test.ts) is consistent with this (it also expects ADHD_AGENT_ANTHROPIC_SECRET set directly) but nothing wires a real token into it by default. Discovered while running a controlled dispatch-mechanism A/B test that needed a raw (harness-free) Anthropic API baseline via OAuth. Fix is NOT to hardcode a secret value into the tracked .mcp.json - needs a safe passthrough (e.g. the MCP host forwarding a named parent env var, or an explicit local-only override file outside version control).

notes.text: Checked whether ADHD_AGENT_CONFIG (.mcp.json env, points at .adhd/agent-mcp/config.json) could carry the secret instead - ruled out. That file exists, is gitignored (.gitignore:79), but only holds `plugins` config (agent-mcp-budget caps/overrides); AgentMcpConfig's actual interface has no `providers`/secret field at all (db, logging, queue, server, transport, sse, plugins only). Provider credentials really are process.env-only with no config-file path, confirming the original finding. Any fix needs to get ADHD_AGENT_ANTHROPIC_SECRET into the agent-mcp server process's own env at spawn time (e.g. .mcp.json env passthrough from a parent-scoped var, or the MCP host forwarding it) - not a file-based route.

Root cause is also a stale doc, not just missing wiring: README.md:55 documents ANTHROPIC_API_KEY as the anthropic-provider credential env var. Traced the real resolution chain end-to-end - AnthropicProvider constructor (packages/agent/agent-engine-orchestrator/src/providers/anthropic.ts:196-209) calls config.getProviderConfig(), which resolves ONLY via env.resolveEnvName(opts.secret ?? PROVIDER_DEFAULTS.anthropic.secret) where that default is "ADHD_AGENT_ANTHROPIC_SECRET" (entrypoint/agent-mcp/src/config.ts:212). No code path anywhere checks the bare ANTHROPIC_API_KEY name - confirmed by reading buildAnthropicClient and the full getProviderConfig branch. The constructor's own thrown error text (anthropic.ts:203-209) already says the correct name (ADHD_AGENT_ANTHROPIC_SECRET) - only the README is wrong. Fix should update README.md:55 (and the sibling OPENAI_API_KEY/DEEPSEEK row if same issue) to the real ADHD_AGENT_<PROVIDER>_SECRET names, in addition to the .mcp.json passthrough gap already logged.

Doc portion fixed. entrypoint/agent-mcp/README.md and AGENTS.md now: (1) replace the wrong ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/OPENAI_API_KEY/DEEPSEEK_API_KEY/GOOGLE_API_KEY rows with the real ADHD_AGENT_ANTHROPIC_SECRET/ADHD_AGENT_OPENAI_SECRET/ADHD_AGENT_DEEPSEEK_SECRET names, sourced from config.ts's PROVIDER_DEFAULTS; (2) document the OAuth (sk-ant-oat via `claude setup-token`) vs console API key (sk-ant-api) split per buildAnthropicClient's prefix branching; (3) add an explicit 'Provider credentials are NOT part of the @adhd/environment config cascade' section explaining they resolve from process.env only, never a config file, since AgentMcpConfig has no providers field; (4) add a 'Known gap' section documenting this repo's .mcp.json not forwarding any ADHD_AGENT_<PROVIDER>_SECRET, with today's workarounds (export in the launching shell, or use a claudecli-type agent which needs no secret at all) and a pointer back to this backlog item — no fake fix invented, per the ask. Also found and fixed two adjacent doc-accuracy bugs discovered while verifying: AGENTS.md's DB-path env var was documented as ADHD_AGENT_DB_PATH but the real name is ADHD_AGENT_DATABASE_PATH (config.ts:77); and both docs claimed Gemini/DeepSeek as first-class supported providers when only anthropic/openai/claudecli exist as provider types (DeepSeek is reachable only via an openai-type agent with an explicit baseURL override; Gemini has zero implementation anywhere in code) — corrected in both files, deeper architecture-doc version of the same issue (architecture-and-security.md's provider table) filed separately as agent-mcp-002 since it's out of scope for this pass. Confirmed via git history why claudecli.ts never captured usage - not a regression, scoped out from the start. Commit b35075ee ("provider-neutral token accounting", BUG-ORCH-009/010) introduced usage/rawUsage/normaliseAnthropicUsage but its diff only touches anthropic.ts and openai.ts (git show --stat confirms); the commit message explicitly scopes the work to "the OpenAI/DeepSeek path" and Anthropic's cache-headline reconciliation - claudecli is never mentioned. claudecli.ts hand-parses raw stream-json lines against its own narrower ClaudeStreamResultEvent type rather than using an SDK's typed response, so nobody declared the usage field that the real CLI apparently already emits on the terminal result event (verified live 2026-07-25: a real `claude -p ... --output-format stream-json` run's result event included usage:{input_tokens,output_tokens,cache_read_input_tokens,cache_creation_input_tokens}, total_cost_usd, and a modelUsage breakdown). The .mcp.json credential-passthrough gap (Condition F, separate issue) remains open and unrelated to this fix.

content:
architecture-and-security.md overstates Gemini/DeepSeek as first-class providers

`entrypoint/agent-mcp/docs/architecture-and-security.md` lines 31-35 ("Provider Adapters" system-boundary diagram) and lines 190-197 ("Provider-Specific Differences" table) present Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, and Gemini as four equally-implemented provider adapters with detailed per-provider caching/streaming/cancellation behavior.

Verified against code while fixing README.md/AGENTS.md credential docs (this pass, see agent-mcp-001): there are exactly 3 provider `type`s in `packages/agent/agent-engine-orchestrator/src/validation/agent.ts` (`anthropic`, `openai`, `claudecli`)[1]. `createProvider()` in `packages/agent/agent-engine-orchestrator/src/providers/factory.ts` switches on only those 3 types[2]. There is no `gemini.ts` provider file anywhere in `packages/agent/agent-engine-orchestrator/src/providers/`[3], no `gemini` reference in `context-window.ts`'s model-context-size table (which does list `deepseek-v4`/`deepseek`)[4], and `config.ts`'s `PROVIDER_DEFAULTS` has no `gemini` entry either (only `openai`/`anthropic`/`deepseek`)[5]. DeepSeek is reachable only by configuring an `openai`-type agent with an explicit `env.base_url` override pointing at DeepSeek's OpenAI-compatible endpoint — not as a first-class `type`.

This doc's per-provider claims for Gemini (cache pricing, tool-definition format, cancellation, streaming) are therefore fabricated/aspirational, not grounded in any implementation. Also worth checking: `entrypoint/agent-mcp/docs/provider-call-audit.md` cites source paths under the dead `packages/ai/agent-mcp/...` tree (e.g. line 14, 36) rather than the current `packages/agent/agent-engine-orchestrator` / `entrypoint/agent-mcp` locations — likely stale from before a package move, per the `packages/ai/*` dead-path warning in the repo's AGENTS.md.

Out of scope for the credential-doc fix pass (agent-mcp-001) which only covered README.md/AGENTS.md's env-var and provider-type tables (now corrected). This item is the broader architecture-doc correction.

content:
claudecli provider silently discarded real token usage from the CLI's own result event

packages/agent/agent-engine-orchestrator/src/providers/claudecli.ts drives the real `claude` binary via `-p --output-format stream-json`. The terminal `result` event on that stream already carries a fully-aggregated `usage` object (input_tokens/output_tokens/cache_read_input_tokens/cache_creation_input_tokens), plus total_cost_usd and a per-model modelUsage breakdown - computed by the CLI itself. But ClaudeStreamResultEvent only ever declared type/subtype/is_error/result, so `JSON.parse(line) as ClaudeStreamEvent` silently dropped the usage field on every claudecli-provider task. ProviderChatResponse.usage/rawUsage were never populated for this provider (unlike anthropic.ts/openai.ts, which do). Root cause traced via git history: commit b35075ee ("provider-neutral token accounting", BUG-ORCH-009/010) introduced usage/rawUsage/normaliseAnthropicUsage but its diff only touches anthropic.ts and openai.ts - claudecli.ts was never in scope for that effort, not a regression. Real-world effect: mcp__agent-mcp__usage_query recorded all-zero tokens (inputTokens:0, cacheReadTokens:null, stopReason:"unknown") for every claudecli-provider task, hiding real spend. Discovered and fixed while running a controlled dispatch-mechanism A/B test that needed real claudecli-provider cost data.

FIX APPLIED AND VERIFIED (already shipped, uncommitted in this working tree): patched claudecli.ts to declare usage/stop_reason/total_cost_usd on ClaudeStreamResultEvent, capture them when the result event fires, and populate ProviderChatResponse.usage/rawUsage via the existing normaliseAnthropicUsage - additive only, zero change to the CLI invocation/args. Verified three ways: (1) npx nx build agent-engine-orchestrator - clean; (2) npx nx test agent-engine-orchestrator - 88/88 pass including new claudecli-usage.test.ts (2 tests) with a real negative control (reverted the capture line, confirmed the test goes red, restored, confirmed green); (3) live end-to-end against the real built dist/ artifact and a real spawned claude -p subprocess (not mocked) - returned real non-zero usage. Then confirmed live through the FULL stack after a /mcp reload: dispatched a claudecli task before and after the reload and queried mcp__agent-mcp__usage_query directly - same result set shows the pre-reload task with zeros/stopReason:"unknown" and the post-reload task with real inputTokens:43042, cacheReadTokens:17507, cacheCreationTokens:25533, stopReason:"stop" side by side.

Not yet verified: whether the DB/schema layer this feeds into (task_usage grain, session/task/turn aggregation) matches what the active DEBT-AGENTMCP-ACCOUNTING-001 redesign in .worktrees/agent-mcp-usage-accounting expects - that worktree's changes were deliberately not touched by this fix since claudecli.ts was outside its modified-files list.

content:
backlog_client_d_link_related returns {result:null} but does not visibly link the two items

Called mcp__backlog__backlog_client_d_link_related with {repo:"adhd", humanIdA:"agent-mcp-003", humanIdB:"agent-mcp-001"} to cross-link two genuinely related-but-distinct backlog items. The call returned {"result":null} - no error, but also no confirmation of what (if anything) it did.

Verified afterward via mcp__backlog__backlog_client_d_get_item on BOTH items:
- agent-mcp-001's updatedAt was unchanged from before the link_related call (still the timestamp of the last append_note that preceded it) - if the link had written anything to either item, updatedAt should have moved.
- Neither item's get_item response includes any related-items/linkedItems/relatedTo field at all, so there's no way to confirm the link exists even if it were stored somewhere not surfaced by get_item.

Either: (a) link_related is a silent no-op / not actually implemented server-side, (b) it succeeded but writes to a field get_item doesn't return (in which case get_item should surface it, since there's no other way for a caller to verify a link took effect), or (c) I'm missing some required param/precondition and the tool should have errored instead of returning a bare null. Whichever it is, a caller currently has no way to confirm this operation did anything - the tool should either return a non-null confirmation (e.g. the updated item(s), or an explicit success/linked-ids payload) or get_item should expose related items so the effect is independently verifiable.

Worked around by adding plain-text cross-references via append_note on both items instead (see agent-mcp-003 and agent-mcp-001 notes, adhd repo).

Verified afterward via mcp__backlog__backlog_client_d_get_item on BOTH items:
- agent-mcp-001's updatedAt was unchanged from before the link_related call (still the timestamp of the last append_note that preceded it) - if the link had written anything to either item, updatedAt should have moved.
- Neither item's get_item response includes any related-items/linkedItems/relatedTo field at all, so there's no way to confirm the link exists even if it were stored somewhere not surfaced by get_item.

Either: (a) link_related is a silent no-op / not actually implemented server-side, (b) it succeeded but writes to a field get_item doesn't return (in which case get_item should surface it, since there's no other way for a caller to verify a link took effect), or (c) I'm missing some required param/precondition and the tool should have errored instead of returning a bare null. Whichever it is, a caller currently has no way to confirm this operation did anything - the tool should either return a non-null confirmation (e.g. the updated item(s), or an explicit success/linked-ids payload) or get_item should expose related items so the effect is independently verifiable.

Worked around by adding plain-text cross-references via append_note on both items instead (see agent-mcp-003 and agent-mcp-001 notes, adhd repo).

content:
usage_query MCP tool's live schema is missing grain param that's already staged in source

entrypoint/agent-mcp/src/server.ts (lines ~370-375, ~551-556) already documents and wires a `grain='session'|'task'|'turn'` parameter for the usage_query tool, dispatching to usageQuery() vs usageQueryByGrain() (packages/agent/agent-engine-orchestrator/src/tools/usage.ts, dispatch fn at line ~140) depending on whether group_by or grain is supplied. usage.ts itself has ~429 new lines implementing session/task/turn grain rows (sessionGrainRows, taskGrainRows, summariseGrainRows, context_size/context_size_at tracking, est_cost_usd), referencing DESIGN.md §2-§4 and DEBT-AGENTMCP-ACCOUNTING-001.

BUT: the live mcp__agent-mcp__usage_query tool schema (re-fetched via ToolSearch this session, after an unrelated /mcp reload) still shows only the OLD parameter set - agent_name, group_by, include_incomplete, limit, root_task_id, since, task_id - no grain param at all, and calling with grain has not been tested/confirmed to work.

Root cause traced (not guessed): git status --short shows both server.ts and usage.ts are STAGED (git add'd, M in the index column) but NOT committed in the main working tree - this is a substantial, deliberate, in-progress body of work (463 lines total) that I did not author and have not touched, discovered while investigating a separate issue (agent-mcp-003). entrypoint/agent-mcp/dist/src/index.js predates these staged source changes (mtime before server.ts's mtime) and contains zero occurrences of the string "grain" - so even if the staged code is complete and correct, the running server process has not been rebuilt/restarted to include it, meaning the live tool cannot expose grain regardless of the source's readiness.

No fix attempted or suggested here - this is a status/visibility gap, not a bug to patch: whoever owns the staged server.ts/usage.ts work needs to finish, build, and commit it (or explicitly abandon it) themselves. Filing so the discrepancy between "what the source already does" and "what the live tool actually exposes" is tracked, since it could otherwise look like the grain feature doesn't exist at all to anyone only checking the live MCP tool schema.

content:
rate-card estimateCostUsd() model-key lookup fails for every real provider-reported model string

packages/agent/agent-core-provider/src/pricing/rate-card.ts's estimateCostUsd(model, usage) is a bare RATE_CARD[model] object lookup with zero normalization - const rate = RATE_CARD[model]; if (!rate) return null. RATE_CARD's keys are underscored canonical names: claude_sonnet_4_6, claude_opus_4_8, claude_haiku_4_5, claude_fable_5, deepseek-v4-flash, deepseek-v4-pro.

But every real caller passes a real, provider-reported or user-configured model string, which is never in that format:
- usage-plugin.ts:108 reads model from the agent's own provider.model config (whatever a human/agent literally typed when creating the agent - e.g. "claude-haiku-4-5", "claude-sonnet-5", or a bare alias like "haiku").
- usage.ts:584 reads model = info.usage.model - the provider-reported string, which for claudecli is the CLI's own dated snapshot id (verified live this session: "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001").

Empirically verified by actually running the real function (npx tsx against the real source, not inferred):
estimateCostUsd("claude-sonnet-5", ...) -> null
estimateCostUsd("claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", ...) -> null
estimateCostUsd("claude-haiku-4-5", ...) -> null
estimateCostUsd("haiku", ...) -> null
estimateCostUsd("sonnet", ...) -> null
estimateCostUsd("claude_sonnet_4_6", ...) -> 0.001185  (only the exact canonical key works)

rate-card.test.ts's own test suite never once exercises a real hyphenated/dated model string - every test passes the canonical underscored key directly, so this never surfaced there. Also notable: RATE_CARD has no claude_sonnet_5 entry at all (only claude_sonnet_4_6), so even a caller that correctly guessed the underscore convention for the current model generation would still get null.

Practical effect once this merged (DEBT-AGENTMCP-ACCOUNTING-001 / .worktrees/agent-mcp-usage-accounting) code is built and deployed: task_usage.est_cost_usd will be null for essentially all real production tasks, any provider - not a claudecli-specific gap, a general one. This is exactly the same class of bug independently found and fixed multiple times this session in a different tool (scratch-claude-metadata's own cost estimator, which needed a _split_model/_resolve_family normalization layer for the identical reason - bare aliases and full dated model ids not matching a hardcoded pricing table).

Not fixed here - discovered while investigating whether agent-mcp-004's grain-accounting merge correctly pulls in claudecli usage specifically; this turned out to be a separate, broader, unrelated-to-claudecli bug. Related: agent-mcp-003 (claudecli usage capture, fixed), agent-mcp-004 (grain feature not yet built/live).

PROBLEM PATTERN (confirmed twice independently in this session, in two unrelated codebases): a pricing/cost table keyed by one exact string format silently fails against the several DIFFERENT formats a model name actually appears in across a real system - bare alias, current canonical id, dated runtime snapshot id, and whatever ad-hoc key convention the table's author picked. scratch-claude-metadata (~/dev/ai/scratch/claude-metadata) hit and fixed the identical class of bug earlier the same day (agent_analytics.py's cost estimator) via a _split_model()/_resolve_family() normalization layer that resolves any input string down to a FAMILY (opus/sonnet/haiku/fable/mythos), then prices by family rather than by exact string match. Recommend the same architecture here: normalize-to-family, not exact-string-match.

RECOMMENDED SHAPE:
```ts
// packages/agent/agent-core-provider/src/pricing/normalize-model.ts
export function normalizeModelKey(raw: string): string | null {
  const s = raw.trim().toLowerCase();
  // 1. bare alias -> current canonical family
  const ALIASES: Record<string, string> = {
    haiku: 'claude_haiku_4_5', sonnet: 'claude_sonnet_4_6' /* or _5 once added, see below */,
    opus: 'claude_opus_4_8', fable: 'claude_fable_5', mythos: 'claude_fable_5',
  };
  if (ALIASES[s]) return ALIASES[s];
  // 2. strip a trailing dated snapshot suffix (8 digits) before matching, e.g.
  //    claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 -> claude-haiku-4-5
  const noDate = s.replace(/-\d{8}$/, '');
  // 3. hyphen -> underscore, since RATE_CARD's Claude keys are underscored
  //    (but its DeepSeek keys are hyphenated - pick ONE convention and migrate
  //    RATE_CARD to it rather than normalizing inputs two different ways)
  const key = noDate.replace(/-/g, '_');
  return key in RATE_CARD ? key : null; // still null (never 0) if truly unrecognized
}
```

[triage] flag=debug-triage route=debugger
Route reason: Confirmed agent-runner.ts spawns a subprocess via StdioClientTransport and has a client.close() cleanup path, but orchestrator.ts has no finally block or SIGINT/SIGTERM handler visible in the code I read guaranteeing that path runs on every early-exit route. Root cause (which specific exit paths actually leak) is genuinely uncertain without tracing every call site, so this needs debugger-lane investigation rather than an architect spec written on assumption.
Priority rationale: Resource-leak-on-abnormal-exit edge case, not a functional blocker; LOW as filed looks correctly scoped.
CAVEAT: 82% of triage agents in this run had NO backlog tool access and reasoned from prompt-inlined data. Treat triage lines as unverified.

[debugger lane] verdict=VERIFIED_LIVE
Evidence: No `.close()` call and no try/finally exist anywhere in the real-runner production path. entrypoint/dispatch-cli/src/lib/core.ts:231-251 (runCycleCore) and :346-373 (calibrateCore) both build `buildProductionAgentMcpRunner()` (a real AgentMcpRunner spawning `npx -y @adhd/agent-mcp` via StdioClientTransport, packages/dispatch/dispatch-orchestrator/src/lib/agent-runner.ts:304-324) and never close it. entrypoint/dispatch-cli/src/api.ts:150-198 (run/calibrate) are pass-throughs with no cleanup. `grep -n 'process.exit\|\.close()' entrypoint/dispatch-cli/bin/cli.ts` returns only `process.exit(1)` inside `fail()` at line 57 — no `.close()`, no finally, no SIGINT/SIGTERM handler in the whole file. agent-runner.ts:446-450's own doc comment says close() is 'not part of IDispatchAgentRunner... callers and tests own this lifecycle step,' but the only caller that does it is test-only code: entrypoint/dispatch-cli/src/test/integration/real-e2e.ts:990-1084 (`finally { if (runner) await runner.close(); }` on a runner it constructs itself for the test).
Recommended action: Root cause confirmed and scoped more broadly than the title: the leak happens on EVERY real invocation (success or failure), not just early exit — because printAndExit() in bin/cli.ts never calls process.exit(0), a successful `dispatch-cli run --no-dry-run`/`calibrate` will hang forever (spawned child's open stdio pipes keep the event loop alive), and on the `fail()` error path the child becomes an orphan since process.exit(1) doesn't tear down non-detached spawned children. Fix: wrap the real-AgentMcpRunner branches of runCycleCore/calibrateCore (or their bin/cli.ts callers) in try/finally calling runner.close(), and add process.exit(0) after a successful printAndExit(). Ready to hand to architect/devops for the actual patch — this is a clear, scoped fix, not a design question.
(The debugger lane HAD shell access; its evidence is reproducible.)"}],"createdAt":"2026-07-25T02:40:15.309Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-20T21:09:08.235Z","priority":"MEDIUM"}

content:
Doc Steward System: programmatic coverage report tool and automated unverifiable-item filing

The doc-steward system (as defined in the system prompt for the steward agent) needs two capabilities:

1. **Programmatic coverage report tool**: The cartographer currently produces metrics.md/doc-conformance.md manually. It needs a tool that computes a structured coverage report: which capabilities have documented verified_output, which have matching README sections, which are missing from user-facing docs, with a numeric coverage score that can trend over time.

2. **Automated unverifiable-item filing**: When the cartographer encounters a capability that CANNOT be verified (missing tool, no TTY, broken dist, etc.), it should automatically file a backlog item with:
   - The exact verify command attempted
   - The error/output received
   - The root cause of WHY it cannot be verified (not just "needs TTY" but "nx generator dry-run requires interactive terminal which is unavailable in non-TTY CI context")
   - A reference to the required-tooling.md entry if a tool is missing

This prevents UNVERIFIED capabilities from accumulating silently in capabilities.json across runs.

meta_parsed.body:
The doc-steward system (as defined in the system prompt for the steward agent) needs two capabilities:

1. **Programmatic coverage report tool**: The cartographer currently produces metrics.md/doc-conformance.md manually. It needs a tool that computes a structured coverage report: which capabilities have documented verified_output, which have matching README sections, which are missing from user-facing docs, with a numeric coverage score that can trend over time.

2. **Automated unverifiable-item filing**: When the cartographer encounters a capability that CANNOT be verified (missing tool, no TTY, broken dist, etc.), it should automatically file a backlog item with:
   - The exact verify command attempted
   - The error/output received
   - The root cause of WHY it cannot be verified (not just "needs TTY" but "nx generator dry-run requires interactive terminal which is unavailable in non-TTY CI context")
   - A reference to the required-tooling.md entry if a tool is missing

This prevents UNVERIFIED capabilities from accumulating silently in capabilities.json across runs.

content:
Log failed apigen calls, failed startup, and errors to disk for usage debugging

Apigen currently logs errors to stderr (pino) but does not persist failed calls, startup failures, or runtime errors to disk in a structured way that can be reviewed later.

**Problem**: When a user reports a bug with apigen run/serve/generate, there is no local log trail to diagnose what happened. Errors vanish when the process exits.

**Desired behavior**:
- Failed apigen calls (schema validation failures, dispatch errors, plugin crashes) should be logged to a structured file under ~/.adhd/apigen-cli/logs/ or similar
- Startup failures (config parse errors, missing files, port conflicts) should be captured
- Logs should include: timestamp, command, input payload (sanitized), error code, error message, stack trace, duration
- Log rotation to prevent unbounded disk usage

**Benefit**: Enables post-hoc debugging, usage pattern analysis, and proactive bug discovery without requiring users to reproduce issues with verbose flags.

content:
Doc steward agent that reviews error logs and files bug/usability issues

Once failed apigen calls and errors are persisted to disk (FEAT-APIGEN-024), add a doc steward agent that periodically reviews those logs and files actionable items.

Purpose: Proactive quality, instead of waiting for user bug reports, the steward should discover failure patterns from the logs themselves.

The agent should:
- Scan structured error logs under the configured apigen logs directory
- Group errors by error code, source plugin/command, and input pattern
- File BUG items for new error patterns, regressions where error count is increasing, and stack traces pointing to code paths not previously reported
- File DEBT items for usability issues, e.g. if 50 percent of errors are invalid_argument with confusing messages, that indicates poor UX
- Track trends: error count per week per command, most common failure modes
- Suppress noise: known or expected errors like user typos should be filtered out

Design constraints:
- Read-only on the logs, never modifies them
- Must be runnable on-demand, not a daemon
- Must deduplicate against existing backlog items before filing
- Could be a standalone CLI tool or part of the apigen CLI itself as a log-review command

Refactor agent-mcp entrypoint to use apigen like backlog — CLI as full client + serve command for MCP

The backlog package (@adhd/backlog) demonstrated a successful apigen-driven entrypoint pattern: a single TypeScript client (client.ts) exports all operations, and apigen's extract/composeSchemas/plugin.run pipeline projects them to CLI (Commander), MCP (stdio), and HTTP (Fastify) from one source of truth. Three transports, one code path, no duplication.

agent-mcp currently has its own hand-written MCP server with manual tool registration, a separate HTTP server for SSE/streaming, and no CLI-based client interface for ad-hoc tool calls. This creates:
- Duplicate routing logic between MCP tools and internal dispatch
- No discoverable CLI interface (can't run `agent-mcp spawn-agent --name foo` from a terminal)
- Manual tool registration that drifts from the actual hooks/stores
- No HTTP transport for direct REST-style access

**Desired refactoring**:

1. Extract a client.ts (like backlog's) that exports every agent operation as a plain async function: spawn-agent, list-agents, stop-agent, get-session, list-tools, usage-query, etc.
2. Wire that client into apigen's extract pipeline to auto-generate:
   - CLI: `agent-mcp spawn-agent --name foo --provider ...` (full client interface)
   - MCP: `agent_mcp_spawn_agent` etc. (replacing manual tool registration)
   - HTTP: `POST /agent-mcp/spawn-agent` etc. (replacing the current custom SSE server or complementing it)
3. Add an `agent-mcp serve` command that starts the MCP/HTTP server(s), mirroring backlog serve
4. Keep the existing custom transports (SSE streaming, gateway, etc.) where they add value — the goal is not to delete working code but to eliminate the manual wiring duplication

**Benefits**:
- CLI becomes a full client interface, not just a config tool
- Tool list is always in sync with actual exports (extraction is the source of truth)
- Third transport (HTTP) for free
- Onboarding aligned with backlog's proven pattern — any engineer who understands backlog understands agent-mcp

**Risk**: agent-mcp has complex streaming and lifecycle semantics (SSE, task streaming, HITL) that backlog doesn't. Pure apigen projection may not handle those — they'd stay on the custom path. The refactoring is for the CRUD/query operations, not for streaming.

Doc steward support for conducting research experiments: benchmarking, A/B testing, performance comparisons for advertisable metrics

The claudecli provider A/B test (FEAT-AGENT-001 note) produced a concrete, advertisable result: 5 turns / 0.21 USD / 26.2s vs 28 turns / 0.71 USD / 90.6s for identical work. That data point is now a killer feature in the RELEASE.md. But it was produced ad-hoc by a human, not by a systematic tool that the doc steward can run.

**Problem**: The doc steward currently has no way to produce verifiable performance comparisons, benchmark results, or A/B test data. Every advertisable metric requires a human to manually design, run, and collect the experiment. This means:
- Metrics are rare (only produced when a human is curious enough)
- Metrics are not reproducible (different methodology each time)
- Metrics can't be refreshed (stale data stays in docs because re-running is expensive)
- No regression detection (a refactor that degrades performance goes unnoticed)

**Desired capability**:

The doc steward should be able to conduct controlled experiments and produce structured, citable metrics:

1. **Define experiment**: task description, conditions to compare (provider A vs provider B, toolset scoped vs wildcard, claudecli vs Agent-tool, etc.), measurement dimensions (turns, cost, wall time, token counts, error rate)
2. **Execute**: run each condition in an isolated environment, collect raw measurements
3. **Analyze**: produce a structured result with min/max/mean per condition, deltas between conditions, and a natural-language summary of what the data shows
4. **Cite**: store the result as a citable metric in the doc catalog that the RELEASE.md and capabilities can reference

**Design constraints**:
- Experiments must be reproducible (same task, same conditions → same order-of-magnitude results)
- Must not depend on paid API calls running automatically (experiments that call LLMs should require explicit opt-in or an env flag)
- Results should include confidence indicators (small sample warning, single-run vs repeated, etc.)
- Should not require the steward to have deep domain expertise in benchmarking methodology

**Relation to existing items**:
- FEAT-DOC-STEWARD-001 (programmatic coverage report tool) is the doc-side analogue — that produces coverage metrics, this produces performance metrics
- FEAT-AGENT-001 (agent-mcp apigen refactoring) would benefit from before/after benchmarks driven by this capability

content:
Backlog plugin system: background plugins for enrichment, triggers, hooks, and extensibility

Backlog currently has a flat operational model: 34 individual client.ts functions dispatched via apigen's extract pipeline to three transports. There is no plugin system for cross-cutting concerns.

In contrast, both apigen and agent-mcp have mature plugin architectures:
- Apigen has 10 transport plugins (MCP, Fastify, Express, CLI-output, JSON Schema, OpenAPI, py-flask, py-grpc, health, logger) plus --use Layer plugins for middleware composition
- Agent-mcp has lifecycle hook plugins (budget enforcement via pre/post model request hooks, sanitization via post-tool-call hooks, usage accounting via post-model-response hooks)

**Desired capability**:

Backlog should support pluggable enrichment and triggers that hook into item lifecycle events:

1. **Lifecycle hooks**: Events that plugins can subscribe to:
   - onItemCreated: after a new item is persisted
   - onItemTransitioned: after a status transition
   - onItemClaimed/Released: after claim changes
   - onItemUpdated: after title/body/priority edits
   - onItemResolved: when an item reaches a terminal status
   - onDependencyAdded/Removed: after dependency graph changes

2. **Enrichment plugins**: Post-creation/update processing that augments items:
   - Auto-tagging: extract tags from item body using LLM or rules
   - Auto-priority: suggest priority based on body content, dependencies, or historical patterns
   - Related-item linker: find and suggest links to existing items with similar content
   - Status validator: enforce workflow rules (e.g. cannot transition to FIXED without a citation)
   - Notification: push to external systems (Slack, email, etc.) on specific transitions

3. **Trigger plugins**: Scheduled or event-based actions:
   - Stale-claim escalator: auto-release claims held beyond a configurable timeout
   - Aging report: flag items that haven't been updated in N days
   - SLO breach notifier: warn when a bug's time-in-status exceeds a threshold

4. **Design constraints**:
   - Plugins are async and non-blocking (they must not slow down the primary create/update path)
   - Each plugin runs in a try/catch so one failure doesn't cascade
   - Plugin execution is ordered and configurable per event type
   - Plugin configuration is stored in the backlog graph store (not a separate config file)
   - Plugin system should be minimal: a Plugin interface (name, hooks map, init/shutdown) and a PluginRegistry that the client.ts operations call at the right points

5. **Relation to existing architecture**:
   - Backlog already has an audit-log event system (DERIVED_FROM nodes written on transitions/claims) — this would be a natural consumer of those events
   - The store already supports CAS writes and bounded retries — safe for plugin-side effects
   - Could reuse the agent-plugin-budget pattern (HookRegistry, PluginFactory types) from @adhd/agent-base-types rather than inventing a new plugin interface

**Priority**: MEDIUM — the current flat model is functional. Plugin support becomes important when backlog has external consumers (CI systems, Slack bots, etc.) that need lifecycle reactions.

content:
Turso adapter across all sox stores: multiprocess concurrent writes

Implement a Turso Database (Rust rewrite, tursodatabase/turso) adapter across all sox-ecosystem store packages: sox-graph-store, sox-vector-store, sox-hybrid-search, sox-ingest.

**Motivation**: All sox stores currently use better-sqlite3 (single-process, single-writer). Turso Database offers:
- True row-level MVCC with BEGIN CONCURRENT (intra-process concurrent writes, experimental)
- Multi-process WAL coordination via .tshm sidecar (experimental, v0.6.0+)
- SQLite file format compatibility
- Native vector similarity search (exact: cosine, L2, dot product, Jaccard)
- Async I/O with io_uring on Linux

The existing research in memory (libsql-mvcc-analysis) confirms: libSQL (C fork) has NO MVCC — it inherits SQLite's single-writer model. The MVCC feature is in Turso Database (Rust rewrite), which is the engine to adopt. However, MVCC is EXPERIMENTAL and intra-process only; multi-process WAL serializes writers. The adapter should be phased:

**Phase 0**: DbAdapter interface (already designed) — ensure every store has a clean adapter seam so Turso can be swapped in without touching store logic
**Phase 1**: Turso as default backend for single-process use (better concurrency within a single process via MVCC)
**Phase 2**: Multi-process WAL coordination for multi-CLI-process scenarios (backlog's 20 concurrent CLI processes, agent-mcp multi-instance)
**Phase 3**: Native vector search via Turso's built-in vector index (retire the separate sox-vector-store + embedding journaled approach)

**Constraints**:
- backward compatible with existing better-sqlite3 databases (Turso reads/writes SQLite file format)
- All existing store tests must pass with both backends
- The adapter seam must not leak Turso-specific types into store logic
- Multi-process WAL must be opt-in (experimental, not default)
- CI must run N-process integrity tests with both backends

Depends on prior research: memory has comprehensive libsql-mvcc-analysis (verified July 2026) covering Turso vs libSQL distinction, MVCC limitations, and multi-process WAL coordination.

See also: FEAT-BACKLOG-001 (backlog plugin system) could consume this for concurrent enrichment plugins, and FEAT-AGENT-001 (agent-mcp apigen entrypoint) could benefit from multi-process DB access.

content:
Configurable composite store server: register/attach DBs on the fly, cross-SQLite-DB joins via composite interface

**Follow-up to**: FEAT-SOX (Turso adapter across all stores)

**Vision**: A configurable composite store server where individual SQLite database files (each potentially backed by a different sox store — graph-store, vector-store, hybrid-search, ingest) can be registered and attached on the fly, then queried through a single composite interface.

**Key capability**: Cross-SQLite-DB-file joins. Currently each sox store opens its own SQLite file and there is no way to query across them (e.g. "find all graph nodes whose vector embeddings are similar to X" requires two separate queries and manual join in application code).

**Required research before implementation**:
1. Read memory research on Turso Database's multi-process WAL coordination (.tshm sidecar) and MVCC architecture — already documented in libsql-mvcc-analysis
2. **Dispatch a research agent** specifically on: Turso's ATTACH/DETACH support for cross-SQLite-DB-file joins — does Turso's Rust rewrite support `ATTACH DATABASE` like SQLite? Does it support cross-file joins with MVCC isolation? What are the performance characteristics vs in-process joins?
3. Investigate: can the composite server run as a sidecar process that multiple CLI tools connect to via Turso's libSQL server protocol, avoiding multi-process WAL contention entirely?

**Composite server design**:
- A lightweight server process (Node.js or Rust via napi) that loads multiple sox store files
- DBs registered via config or runtime API call
- Clients connect via libSQL protocol (SQL wire-compatible) or a simpler JSON-RPC interface
- The server handles cross-file joins transparently
- Optional: hot-attach (add a DB file without restarting the server)

**Relation to existing architecture**:
- sox-executor design (in memory) already specifies a DbAdapter seam with phased Turso adoption
- This feature builds on Phase 2+ of that plan (multi-process coordination)
- FEAT-BACKLOG-001 (backlog plugin system) could be a consumer — enrichment plugins could attach additional DBs
- agent-mcp's multi-instance SSE contention fix (BUG-AGENTMCP-003) shows demand for shared-state coordination patterns

**Priority**: MEDIUM — requires Turso adapter (FEAT-SOX) to exist first, plus research outcome on cross-file join support.

1. Read memory research on Turso Database's multi-process WAL coordination (.tshm sidecar) and MVCC architecture — already documented in libsql-mvcc-analysis
2. **Dispatch a research agent** specifically on: Turso's ATTACH/DETACH support for cross-SQLite-DB-file joins — does Turso's Rust rewrite support `ATTACH DATABASE` like SQLite? Does it support cross-file joins with MVCC isolation? What are the performance characteristics vs in-process joins?
3. Investigate: can the composite server run as a sidecar process that multiple CLI tools connect to via Turso's libSQL server protocol, avoiding multi-process WAL contention entirely?

**Composite server design**:
- A lightweight server process (Node.js or Rust via napi) that loads multiple sox store files
- DBs registered via config or runtime API call
- Clients connect via libSQL protocol (SQL wire-compatible) or a simpler JSON-RPC interface
- The server handles cross-file joins transparently
- Optional: hot-attach (add a DB file without restarting the server)

**Relation to existing architecture**:
- sox-executor design (in memory) already specifies a DbAdapter seam with phased Turso adoption
- This feature builds on Phase 2+ of that plan (multi-process coordination)
- FEAT-BACKLOG-001 (backlog plugin system) could be a consumer — enrichment plugins could attach additional DBs
- agent-mcp's multi-instance SSE contention fix (BUG-AGENTMCP-003) shows demand for shared-state coordination patterns

**Priority**: MEDIUM — requires Turso adapter (FEAT-SOX) to exist first, plus research outcome on cross-file join support.

content:
Cross-repository backlog graph via composite store server

**Depends on**: FEAT-SOX-002 (composite store server for cross-DB joins)

**Vision**: Currently each backlog instance has its own SQLite graph store scoped to a single repo. Items from different repos are completely isolated — there is no way to query across repos, link items across repos, or see a unified view of work spanning multiple repositories.

The composite store server (FEAT-SOX-002) provides exactly the infrastructure needed: a server that can ATTACH multiple SQLite DB files and query across them with SQL joins. Backlog can use this to build a cross-repository graph.

**How it works**:

1. Each repository's backlog store is a standard sox-graph-store SQLite file (already the case — backlog uses @adhd/sox-graph-store)
2. The composite store server loads multiple store files: one per repo, plus a global cross-repo index
3. Clients connect to the composite server (via libSQL protocol or JSON-RPC) instead of opening their own store file directly
4. The server exposes cross-repo operations:
   - `list-items --all-repos`: unified view across all loaded repos
   - `link-across-repos --repo-a ... --human-id ... --repo-b ... --human-id ...`: create dependency/relation edges between items in different repos
   - `cross-repo-blockers`: find all blockers across repos for a given team/area
   - `spanning-tree`: dependency graph that crosses repo boundaries

**Under the hood**:
- Each repo's store file is ATTACHed to the composite server with an alias (e.g. `repo_adhd`, `repo_ai`, `repo_sox`)
- Cross-repo edges are stored in a separate cross-repo index file (also ATTACHed) with source_repo + target_repo columns
- Queries use SQL UNION ALL or cross-file JOINs via the server, which handles them transparently
- This is the same mechanism as `ATTACH DATABASE` in SQLite, just routed through the composite server so multi-process clients don't contend on file locks

**Backward compatibility**:
- Single-repo mode remains the default (open your own store file directly, no server needed)
- Cross-repo mode is opt-in: `backlog serve --composite --config repos.json`
- Existing single-repo CLI commands work unchanged against the composite server (it speaks the same interface)

**Broader significance**: This is the architecture that makes backlog viable as an organization-wide coordination tool, not just a per-repo bug tracker. A team working across 5 repos sees one graph, one query surface, one set of cross-repo blockers.

content:
Migrate memory bundle vector store to Turso native vector search

The memory server at sox-ecosystem/extensions/bundles/memory currently uses sox-vector-store for embedding storage and similarity search, with a journaled approach: embeddings are written to a separate SQLite file and queried via brute-force or filtered-knn. This adds complexity (two storage systems to maintain, embedding journal for durability, separate vector store lifecycle).

Turso Database (Rust rewrite, tursodatabase/turso) has built-in vector similarity search:
- Native vector column type with index
- Exact search: cosine, L2, dot product, Jaccard similarity
- Filters on arbitrary columns combined with vector search in a single query
- SQLite file format compatible — existing data can be migrated in-place

**What migrating means**:
- Memory nodes that carry embeddings would store them directly in the graph store's Turso-backed table as a native vector column, rather than in a separate sox-vector-store file
- Similarity search becomes a SQL query with an ORDER BY vector_distance() clause instead of a separate search() call
- The embedding journal (write-ahead for vector durability) can be retired — Turso's WAL serves that purpose natively
- Filtered-knn becomes a native WHERE + vector ORDER BY, not a JOIN workaround

**Dependency chain**:
- Depends on FEAT-SOX-001 (Turso adapter across all sox stores) — the DbAdapter seam must exist for sox-graph-store first
- Depends on Turso's vector search being stable enough for the memory server's recall/query workload
- The memory server's embedding provider (@adhd/sox-embedding-provider or equivalent) would still produce the embedding vectors; only the storage and query layer changes

**Phased approach**:
1. DbAdapter seam in sox-graph-store (Phase 0 of FEAT-SOX-001)
2. Memory bundle opens its graph store via the Turso adapter instead of better-sqlite3
3. Migrate existing vector data: read from sox-vector-store, write to Turso native vector column
4. Switch memory recall queries from sox-vector-store.search() to SQL vector_distance()
5. Retire the sox-vector-store dependency from memory bundle once migration is validated
6. Benchmark: recall latency, recall quality, storage size before/after

**Risk**: Turso's vector search is relatively new. If it doesn't meet recall quality or latency requirements, the memory bundle can fall back to the existing sox-vector-store path via the DbAdapter seam — no regression possible.

**Location**: sox-ecosystem/extensions/bundles/memory/

**See also**: FEAT-SOX-001 (Turso adapter), FEAT-SOX-002 (composite store server), FEAT-BACKLOG-002 (cross-repo backlog graph — same infrastructure).

content:
Standardize backlog CLI flag conventions across all commands

Backlog CLI commands are inconsistent in how they accept arguments. Some use --input <json> (create-item, list-items, import-from-markdown), others use direct flags (--human-id, --repo for get-item, update-item, add-dependency, etc.), and others have positional arguments (install-skill).

This caused real friction during development: I spent multiple round-trips debugging why `--opt input=...` was rejected, then why `--input` accepted JSON but didn't parse humanId correctly, then why `update-item --human-id X --patch Y` worked but `get-item --input {...}` didn't.

**Desired**: A single consistent pattern:
- All commands accept `--input <json>` for the full payload (machine-friendly, deterministic)
- Commonly-used commands also expose direct flags for the most frequent fields (human-friendly, no JSON construction needed for simple cases)
- `--help` for every command shows BOTH forms
- No positional arguments (they break command discovery and are invisible in --help)

This is non-trivial because the CLI is generated by apigen-plugin-cli-output from the extract() schema — the flag shape is determined by the TypeScript function signatures, not manually configured. Fixing consistency may require changes to how apigen generates CLI flags from function parameters.

Available: --by, --human-id, --repo, --text" -- it named the valid set, so it self-corrected in a single retry. That message is the model the other commands should copy.
(3) --help is close to useless for the --input commands: "backlog create-item  { input: object }" is the ENTIRE output. It does not name a single field of that object, so the only way to learn the payload shape is to read the MCP JSON Schema for the sibling tool or to probe live. update-item is the same: "{ repo: string, humanId: string, patch: object }" with no indication of which keys the patch object accepts -- which matters enormously, because most of them are silently dropped (see BUG-BACKLOG-UPDATE-ITEM-SILENT-DISCARD-001).
(4) Flag naming diverges from payload field naming: the CLI flag is --human-id while the JSON field is humanId.
This item's "no positional arguments" and "help shows both forms" clauses are the right fix. Adding a fifth: --help for an --input command must enumerate the object's fields, or the generated CLI is undocumented by construction. Suggest raising priority from LOW -- (3) is what makes the silent-discard bugs so expensive to discover.

Agent type catalog: document available agent types, their tools, and when to use each

The system prompt defines ~20 specialized agent types (architect, researcher, doc-cartographer, doc-consumer, doc-evangelist, doc-reviewer, doc-steward, dispatch-project-implementer-deepseek, dispatch-project-implementer-flash, dispatch-project-orchestrator, dispatch-project-reviewer-flash, dispatcher, explore, general, performance, plan-builder, product, refactor, debug, backend, test, typescript, review).

There is no document explaining what each agent type is for, what tools it has access to, when to dispatch it vs handle the task directly, or which model backs it. Currently the only way to discover these is to read the full system prompt or guess from names.

**Desired**: A catalog document (AGENTS.md section or separate doc) with:
- Agent type name
- Model (deepseek-v4-flash, deepseek-v4-pro, etc.)
- Tools they have access to
- What they're good at (single-file changes, multi-file refactors, read-only research, orchestration, etc.)
- When to dispatch vs handle directly
- Example: "For well-specified simple tasks, use dispatch-project-implementer-flash instead of dispatch-project-implementer-deepseek to save tokens"

This would reduce token waste from dispatching the wrong agent type.

backlog install-skill command is a shipped capability but invisible from --help

The `backlog install-skill` command is a real, working, shipped capability. It was verified working: installed to opencode successfully, SKILL.md copied to the correct path.

But it does NOT appear in `backlog --help` output. It's special-cased in cli.ts before the apigen dispatch loop (because it needs no store/ctx), so the auto-generated help from the apigen route table doesn't include it.

**Impact**: Users cannot discover this command exists. It's a shipped capability that might as well not exist from a discoverability standpoint.

**Fix options**:
1. Add install-skill to the apigen route table with a dummy ctx that throws if called without the real special-case path
2. Override the help output to include it manually
3. Make install-skill a real client.ts operation that takes a ctx but doesn't use it (already possible, the lazy ctx pattern exists)

See also: entrypoint/backlog/src/cli.ts for the special-casing, entrypoint/backlog/src/install-skill.ts for the implementation.

Repository as a first-class node type; decompose backlog item IDs into structured composite keys

Backlog items currently have a `repo` field (string) and a `humanId` field (string like `FEAT-BACKLOG-003`). The humanId encodes multiple dimensions in a flat string: kind (FEAT), family (BACKLOG), sequence number (003). This is brittle and limited.

**Problems**:
1. **Repo is just a string field** — it's not a node. There's no way to store repo metadata (path on disk, remote URL, description, active status). Cross-repo operations require matching on string equality.
2. **humanId is a packed composite key** — Kind, family/component, and sequence are concatenated with hyphens. You can't filter by kind alone, or sequence range, or family. The stats output has to re-parse the humanId to produce byKind/byFamily counts.
3. **Cross-repo linking is impossible** — Dependencies are scoped to (repo, humanId). You can't create a dependency between items in different repos because the current schema has no target_repo field on the dependency edge.

**Desired**:
1. **Repo as a first-class node type** with properties: name (unique), path (filesystem path), remote URL, description, active status. Repos registered via `backlog register-repo --name sox-ecosystem --path ~/dev/ai/sox-ecosystem`.
2. **Decompose humanId** into separate indexed fields: `kind` (BUG/FEAT/DEBT/etc.), `component` (BACKLOG/APIGEN/AGENT/etc.), `sequence` (integer, auto-increment per component). The humanId string is still generated for display but the structured fields are the queryable source of truth.
3. **Dependency edges carry source_repo + target_repo** (or better, reference the repo node directly) so cross-repo dependencies are a first-class operation.

This is a prerequisite for FEAT-BACKLOG-002 (cross-repo backlog graph). Without repo as a node type and structured IDs, cross-repo queries will always be string-matching hacks.

content:
Bulk and batch operations for CLI and MCP transports

Backlog currently operates one-item-at-a-time: create-item takes one input, add-dependency takes one pair, transition-status takes one transition, etc. For an agent that needs to file 5 bugs, link them to a plan, and transition them to triaged, that is 7+ sequential tool calls.

This is expensive (each call is an MCP round-trip, each CLI invocation has startup overhead) and slow (serial execution). The apigen extract pipeline generates one operation per exported function, so batch operations require explicit batch functions.

Desired batch operations:
- batch-create-items: takes an array of item inputs, returns array of created items. Atomic: all succeed or all fail.
- batch-transition-status: takes array of repo/humanId/status tuples, atomically transitions all that can transition, reports failures for the rest.
- batch-add-dependencies: takes array of repo/humanId/dependsOn tuples.
- import-batch: high-volume import from JSON or CSV with progress reporting for large sets over 100 items.

MCP considerations:
- MCP tools have output size limits. A batch create of 100 items returning full details could exceed transport limits. Batch operations should have a summary mode (return created count and errors array) and a verbose mode (return full items).
- The MCP transport should support streaming responses for large batches or paginated results.

CLI considerations:
- --input already accepts JSON. A batch operation would accept --input with the items array.
- For shell usage, could also accept --file items.jsonl for large imports without loading everything into argv.

content:
Doc steward should auto-verify link integrity at write time, not as a separate step

During RELEASE.md composition, all relative links needed manual post-hoc verification with a script. The steward should verify link integrity at write time — before committing a doc that contains relative links.

**Problem**: A doc with dead links is worse than no doc. A user clicking a reference and hitting 404 loses trust immediately. The steward system prompt already has a reviewer rule about dead links being a hard FAIL, but the steward writes the doc and the reviewer catches it later — creating a fix loop.

**Desired**: Before every write/create operation on a doc file that contains relative Markdown links, the steward should:
1. Parse all relative links from the content
2. Resolve each against the file's own directory
3. If any link doesn't resolve, either fix it (if the target exists under a different path) or block the write with an error listing every broken link

This should be zero-effort for the steward — a built-in integrity check before any doc write, not a separate verification step to remember.

content:
Doc steward should write docs within individual project doc trees, not all at repo root

The steward currently writes all scope-level docs to the repo root: README.md, CHANGELOG.md, RELEASE.md, AGENTS.md. For a monorepo with 54 published packages and 7 domains, this creates a flat root with files that belong in their respective project directories.

**Problem**: Capabilities like the backlog usage skill (which documents how to use a specific package) end up referenced from the root RELEASE.md but the actual usage skill file lives in the backlog package. Comparison guides, performance benchmarks, and domain-specific docs should live alongside the packages they describe.

**Desired**: The steward should place docs in the package or domain they describe, not at the repo root:
- Root README.md: navigation map only (what exists, where to find it, quick-start links)
- Root RELEASE.md: executive summary + cross-cutting themes (build tooling, workspace hygiene) — domain-specific release notes go in their own packages
- Package-level docs: per-package README.md, CHANGELOG.md, AGENTS.md, skill files (already the pattern for backlog, agent-mcp)
- Domain-level docs: docs/agent/, docs/apigen/, docs/dispatch/ — per-domain architecture and comparison guides

The monolithic root README/RELEASE approach is a monorepo anti-pattern. It works for a single package but collapses in a multi-domain workspace where each domain has its own audience, release cadence, and documentation needs.

content:
Blast radius enrichment for backlog item citations

When a backlog item has citations referencing source files, the backlog should auto-enrich it with blast radius data: what packages those files belong to, what other items reference the same files, and what the impact scope is.

Problem: A bug is filed with a citation like packages/apigen/apigen-core-client/src/lib/extract.ts. The reader has to manually figure out what package that is, what other items touch the same file, whether this is a core utility change (wide blast radius) or a leaf change (narrow).

Desired enrichment on citation add:
1. Resolve each cited file path to its npm package name from the directory structure
2. Determine package tier or domain from project.json tags
3. Cross-reference against other items with overlapping file citations
4. Estimate blast radius: base/core tier equals HIGH, plugin/entrypoint equals LOW, configurable
5. Store as structured metadata: affectedPackages, affectedFiles, blastRadius (low/medium/high/critical), relatedItems

Query surface:
- list-items with filter by affectedPackage: @adhd/apigen-core-client
- list-items with filter by blastRadius: HIGH
- list-items with filter by affectedFile matching pattern

Integration with FEAT-BACKLOG-001 (plugin system): this would be the first enrichment plugin. onItemCreated and onItemUpdated hooks call a blast-radius resolver service that could use GitNexus impact analysis under the hood.

content:
Clustering queries with filtered group-bys for dimensional backlog analysis

Backlog currently supports flat list-items with filters and stats which does basic byKind/byFamily aggregation. There is no way to ask dimensional questions like:
- What are all the tasks on agent packages that touch index.ts?
- What are all claude-agents bugs that touch doc-steward.md or workflow-agent-builder.md?
- What are all agent-mcp related bugs across any repo?
- What are all unblocked items touching a specific file path?
- Which packages have the most open bugs?
- How many HIGH priority items per component?
- Which files are cited by the most backlog items?

Desired: A flexible query operation combining:
1. Filters: byKind, byPriority, byStatus, byRepo, byHumanId pattern, byDate range, byCitedFile, byAffectedPackage, byCitationText
2. Group-by dimensions: kind, component, priority, status, repo, affectedPackage, citedFile, week or month of createdAt
3. Aggregations: count, countDistinct, oldest, newest, priority distribution, status distribution
4. Sort: by any dimension ascending or descending
5. Output formats: table (markdown), JSON, CSV, count-only, list-of-ids

Examples:

content:
apigen CLI --input should also support --file to bypass shell escaping issues

Every apigen-generated CLI command that accepts --input with raw JSON on the command line. This is inherently fragile: single quotes in body text, backslash escapes, dollar signs, and parentheses all cause shell expansion or JSON parse failures.

This session alone had 5+ failed create-item calls due to shell/JSON escaping issues. Every time the workaround was to write the JSON to a temp file and read it back.

A --file flag that reads JSON from a file would bypass all shell escaping issues. --input and --file should be mutually exclusive. --file should accept both regular JSON and JSONL for batch imports.

This applies to every apigen-generated CLI command: backlog create-item, list-items, update-item, etc.

content:
54 published packages have empty or missing package.json descriptions

Every published @adhd/* package has a description field in its package.json. During the steward's capability audit, 14 packages had empty descriptions requiring source-code inspection to understand their purpose.

Description-less packages: apigen-base-errors, apigen-base-logical, apigen-base-schema, apigen-base-types, apigen-codegen-openapi, apigen-engine-conformance, apigen-engine-gateway, apigen-engine-runtime, apigen-generator-nx, apigen-python-env, decompile-cli, dispatch-base-types, ui-react-base-hooks, workspace-base-tools.

npm view, npm search, and every package registry UI shows the description as blank. This is a discoverability tax on every new contributor and every automated tool.

Fix: Add a one-sentence description to each package.json, sourced from what the package actually exports. Descriptions should be in the source package.json (not just dist) so they ship with npm publish.
